The simple area-to-speed ratio v₂/v₁=A₁/A₂ requires equal volume flow rate at the two sections in an incompressible no-leak model; pressure equality is not required.
Gravity increases speed of a freely falling water jet; for nearly unchanged volumetric rate, A=Q/v decreases. Fragmentation/splashing would limit that simple picture.
The question expressly fixes equal discharge, so twice the effective flow area means half the mean speed. Deeper water alone, without comparable section discharge, would not guarantee slower flow.
Under steady incompressible splitting without sources/storage between sections, 12−5=7 m³/s in the second channel; original A is correct.

teacher_review_theme: Fifty equal-size vessels but no equal discharge
teacher_scientific_note: Flow conservation and equal branch radii only constrain the SUM of 50 discharge rates, not each branch's velocity. Source A 0.40 m/s follows only if equal discharge is expressly assumed. Other distributions with distinct branch velocities also satisfy continuity. Add an equal-split condition before individually certified exam use.

teacher_review_theme: Three-outlet rate balance and PDF superscript
teacher_scientific_note: 6−2−2=2 L/s for the third exit, original B, assuming no loss/storage. The PDF visually displays Q68 'L s⁻¹' correctly; extracted text misplaced the superscript, not an original bank transcription error.
Equal-area readings 2 and 3 m/s cannot both match steady incompressible no-leak unbranched water flow. Check meter data or assumptions, not fluid-mass creation.

Steady channel accounting with an added side supply requires mass inflow from that source. For equal-density water, Q_down=Q_up+Q_side minus other losses; cross-sectional area alone does not fix the speed.
Here the question explicitly states equal splitting, so 9 L/min over three branches gives 3 L/min each. Equal geometric area by itself would not suffice.

teacher_review_theme: Density doubles at fixed A and mass rate
teacher_scientific_note: If ρAv remains unchanged and A is fixed, doubling density halves the mean speed. This is steady mass-throughflow, not an unsteady storage situation.

teacher_review_theme: Aggregate outlet area versus speed in each artery
teacher_scientific_note: Comparing the aorta with the SUM of all branch cross-sectional areas is appropriate to compare aggregate transport; option C remains best. Inferring a particular speed for EACH artery additionally needs a specified distribution of flow, often equal splitting, which should be clarified alongside original Example 6.3.

teacher_review_theme: 1 L per second versus volumetric leak rate
teacher_scientific_note: Upstream 5 L/s minus downstream 4 L/s gives a leak RATE of 1 L/s; option A says 1 L, which is correct as the amount escaping DURING each one-second interval as asked, but is not itself a rate unit. Teacher should decide whether to retain that precise wording or produce a separate improved rate-question option reading 1 L/s; do not silently change original A.

teacher_review_theme: Fixed throughput into a smaller section
teacher_scientific_note: For the given discharge and effective outlet area smaller than tank surface area, section-average outlet speed Q/A is larger. Real tank flow may vary with head; the question fixes discharge for the comparison.
A circular diameter reduced to 70% has area 0.70²=0.49 of original, so average speed ratio 1/0.49≈2.04 if the same volume passes each second.

teacher_review_theme: One-location temporal change ambiguous under steady condition
teacher_scientific_note: Numerical ratio (0.40/0.10)×0.5=2.0 m/s supports source C at equal discharge. But 'at one location in a steady channel, flow area decreases' may indicate a time-varying geometry at a fixed location, conflicting with steady flow during transition. Rephrase as two different channel sections, or distinct steady before/after states at constant Q, before exam certification.

teacher_review_theme: Kinematic displacement not an independent continuity calculation
teacher_scientific_note: Δx=vΔt=2×0.50=1.0 m, source D correct. The problem uses single-element motion rather than mass conservation or the area–speed continuity equation; don't automatically certify as an application of P-11-B-36.

teacher_review_theme: Units of Av are supportive, not application-level continuity
teacher_scientific_note: A[m²]×v[m/s] yields volumetric flow m³/s, so source C correct. This units/definition recognition is Knowledge-level supporting practice, not by itself a B-36 Summative/Application problem.
